question: A DC motor produces rotation because:

options.text: A current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field experiences a force
A changing current in one coil induces a current in a neighbouring coil
A conductor moved through a magnetic field has an EMF induced in it
Two parallel conductors carrying current in the same direction repel each other

explanation: The force on the armature conductors (F = BIL, direction from Fleming's left-hand rule) produces torque. The commutator reverses the current in each conductor as it passes between poles, so the torque always acts the same way.

question: The back-EMF generated in a running DC motor:

options.text: Exists only in AC motors and has no effect in DC machines
Adds to the applied voltage and increases the armature current at high speed
Opposes the supply, grows with speed and so limits the armature current
Is greatest when the motor is stationary and falls as it speeds up

explanation: A spinning armature is also a generator. Its EMF opposes the supply (Lenz's law), so the current that flows is (V − Eb)/R. At standstill Eb is zero, which is why starting current is so large.

question: A 28 V DC motor has an armature resistance of 0.5 Ω. When running, its back-EMF is 26 V. What is the armature current running, and what would it be at the instant of starting?

options.text: 4 A running; 4 A at the instant of starting
4 A running; 56 A at the instant of starting
56 A running; 4 A at the instant of starting
52 A running; 56 A at the instant of starting

explanation: Running: I = (V − Eb)/R = (28 − 26)/0.5 = 4 A. At the instant of starting the armature is still, Eb = 0, so I = 28/0.5 = 56 A — fourteen times the running current. Heavy motors therefore have starting resistances or current-limited supplies.

question: A DC series-wound motor is well suited to engine starters and actuators because it:

options.text: Runs at a fixed speed set by the supply frequency
Can safely be run with no load connected
Produces a very high starting torque
Runs at an almost constant speed regardless of load

explanation: In a series motor the large starting current flows through both field and armature, giving a very strong field and very high torque from standstill. The trade-off is poor speed regulation.

question: A DC series-wound motor must never be run with no mechanical load because:

options.text: Its direction of rotation reverses when the load is removed
It draws its maximum current when unloaded and burns out its field
Its speed rises without limit and it may destroy itself
It will not start at all without a load

explanation: With no load, the current falls, which weakens the series field; a weaker field means the motor must spin faster to generate enough back-EMF. That runaway can burst the armature. Series motors are therefore always permanently coupled to their load.

question: A DC shunt-wound motor is used where:

options.text: A nearly constant speed is needed under varying load, as with fans and pumps
The speed must vary widely with the load, as with a winch
The motor must run at exactly the speed set by the supply frequency
Very high starting torque is needed, as with engine starters

explanation: With the field across the supply, its flux stays roughly constant whatever the load, so the speed falls only slightly as load increases. Starting torque is moderate.

question: The direction of rotation of a DC motor can be reversed by:

options.text: Increasing the supply voltage beyond its rated value
Reversing the current in either the armature or the field, but not both
Reversing the current in both the armature and the field together
Reversing the polarity of the supply to the whole motor, for any type

explanation: Torque direction depends on both the field direction and the armature current direction. Reverse one and the torque reverses; reverse both and the two reversals cancel. That is why reversing the supply leads of a series or shunt motor does not reverse it.

question: A split-field series motor, used in reversible actuators, has:

options.text: A permanent magnet field and a reversible commutator
Two armatures on one shaft that drive in opposite directions
Two opposite-wound field windings, one selected for each direction
A single field winding that is split by a capacitor to give a rotating field

explanation: Selecting one field winding or the other reverses the field while the armature current stays the same, so a simple changeover switch drives the actuator either way — extend or retract, open or close.

question: An electrical linear actuator, such as one driving a trim tab or flap, is usually stopped at the end of its travel by:

options.text: A timer that switches the motor off after a fixed period
The motor stalling against a mechanical stop until its circuit breaker trips
The back-EMF of the motor rising to equal the supply voltage
Limit switches that cut the motor supply at the end positions

explanation: Limit switches (often microswitches) open the motor circuit when the actuator reaches each end of its travel. Many actuators also have an electromagnetic brake to stop overrun once the supply is cut.

question: An electromagnetic brake fitted to an actuator motor is typically:

options.text: Applied only if the actuator's limit switch fails
Spring-applied when unpowered, and solenoid-released when the motor runs
Applied by a solenoid whenever the motor is powered, and released by a spring
Used only to slow the motor during start-up to reduce its current

explanation: Failing safe to 'brake on' means the actuator stops promptly and holds its position whenever power is removed — at a limit switch, or on a power failure — and cannot be back-driven by air loads.

question: A clutch is often fitted between an actuator motor and its output in order to:

options.text: Increase the output speed above the motor speed
Allow the motor to run with no load while the actuator is at its limit
Reverse the direction of the output without reversing the motor
Slip if the output jams, protecting the motor and gearbox from overload

explanation: A slipping (friction) clutch limits the torque transmitted. If the driven surface jams, the clutch slips instead of stalling the motor or breaking the gear train.

question: During an engine start, the starter motor current is highest:

options.text: Constant throughout the start
Just before the starter disengages, when the engine is turning fastest
Midway through the start, when the engine first fires
At the instant of engagement, before the starter and engine have begun to turn

explanation: At rest the motor has no back-EMF, so only its low resistance limits the current — the large surge that dips the bus voltage at the start. As speed builds, back-EMF rises and the current falls.

question: A three-phase induction motor runs because:

options.text: The rotor is supplied with DC through slip rings and locks to the stator field
Its three-phase stator sets up a rotating field that drags the rotor round
A commutator reverses the rotor current every half cycle
The rotor is a permanent magnet attracted by each phase in turn

explanation: Three windings displaced by 120° and fed with currents 120° apart create a field of constant strength rotating at synchronous speed. It cuts the rotor bars, inducing currents whose field interacts with the rotating field to produce torque — no electrical connection to the rotor is needed.

question: An induction motor always runs slightly slower than the speed of its rotating field because:

options.text: Friction in the bearings prevents it reaching synchronous speed
Without relative motion no rotor current, and so no torque, would be induced
The rotor is locked to the field at half its speed
The supply frequency always falls when the motor is loaded

explanation: If the rotor turned at synchronous speed, its bars would not cut any flux, no current would be induced and there would be no torque. The difference, called slip, increases with load.

question: A four-pole AC motor is supplied at 400 Hz. Its synchronous speed is:
explanation: Synchronous speed = 60 × f / pole pairs = 60 × 400 / 2 = 12,000 rpm. Four poles means two pole pairs; using four instead of two gives 6,000 rpm.

question: The direction of rotation of a three-phase induction motor can be reversed by:

options.text: Reversing the polarity of the DC supply to the rotor
Interchanging any two of the three supply phases
Interchanging all three supply phases in rotation
Reducing the supply frequency to below half its normal value

explanation: Swapping two phases reverses the phase sequence, so the stator field rotates the other way. Rotating all three connections (A→B→C→A) keeps the same sequence and the same direction. A wrong phase sequence from a ground power unit would run every three-phase motor backwards — which is why it is monitored.

question: A lightly loaded three-phase induction motor loses one of its phases while running. The usual result is that it:

options.text: Keeps running at reduced speed, but will not start the next time it is selected
Reverses its direction of rotation
Stops immediately and cannot be damaged
Runs faster, because the remaining phases carry more current

explanation: With one phase gone the stator field no longer rotates smoothly, but a turning motor can keep going — typically at about half speed, humming and drawing extra current. The fault often goes unnoticed in a remote motor until the next start, when it develops no starting torque at all.

question: A synchronous motor differs from an induction motor in that it:

options.text: Runs at exactly the speed of the rotating field, with its speed fixed by the supply frequency
Has its speed set by the supply voltage rather than the frequency
Runs slightly slower than the rotating field, with a slip that increases with load
Needs no AC supply, running on DC through a commutator

explanation: The synchronous motor's rotor is magnetised (by a permanent magnet or DC field) and locks to the rotating field, so it has no slip. It is used where an exact speed proportional to frequency is wanted. It is not self-starting on its own and needs a starting arrangement.

question: A single-phase induction motor needs a starting arrangement, such as a second winding with a capacitor, because:

options.text: The supply voltage of a single phase is too low to turn the rotor
Single-phase AC cannot induce any current in a squirrel-cage rotor
A single phase gives a pulsating, not a rotating, field
A single-phase motor would otherwise run at twice its rated speed

explanation: A single winding gives a field that simply grows and reverses in one axis. A second winding with its current shifted in phase (by a capacitor, for example) adds a component at right angles, producing a rotating field that starts the motor.

question: The rotor of a squirrel-cage induction motor consists of:

options.text: Conducting bars joined by end rings, with no external connection
A permanent magnet with its poles fixed to the shaft
A wound field supplied with DC through slip rings
A wound armature fed through a commutator and carbon brushes

explanation: The cage of bars and end rings is robust and needs no brushes, so the induction motor is simple and reliable — the reason it powers many aircraft fuel pumps, hydraulic pumps and fans running on 115 V 400 Hz.

question: Compared with an AC induction motor, a DC brushed motor has the disadvantage that:

options.text: It cannot produce any torque at standstill
Its speed is fixed by the supply frequency
It cannot have its speed controlled by any means
Its commutator and brushes wear and can spark

explanation: The commutator is the weak point of a brushed DC machine: wear, carbon dust and sparking (a potential ignition source near fuel vapour). Induction motors have no commutator, which is why fuel pumps are commonly AC motors or brushless designs.

question: A stepper motor is characterised by:

options.text: Running continuously at a speed set by the supply voltage
Producing a very high starting torque for engine starting
Running at a speed set only by its load, like a series motor
Turning a fixed angle per input pulse, so pulses set its position

explanation: Each pulse advances the rotor one step. Counting pulses therefore sets position precisely, which suits instrument pointers, valves and other positioning tasks.

question: Many aircraft motors contain a thermal switch in their windings. It is fitted to:

options.text: Indicate on the flight deck that the motor has reached operating temperature
Cut the motor's supply if its windings overheat
Connect a heater to keep the motor warm at altitude
Increase the motor's speed when it gets hot to improve its cooling

explanation: A stalled or overloaded motor draws a large current and heats its windings. A thermal cut-out in the winding breaks the supply before the insulation fails; on some designs it resets automatically when cool.

question: A compound-wound DC motor combines series and shunt fields in order to:

options.text: Reverse its direction automatically when overloaded
Remove the need for a commutator and brushes
Run at a speed set exactly by the supply frequency
Combine strong starting torque with a safe no-load speed

explanation: The series winding gives strong torque at start; the shunt winding provides a field that does not collapse when the load is removed, setting a safe no-load speed.

question: Some DC motors have a resistor switched in series with the armature at start, then bypassed once running. Its purpose is to:

options.text: Limit the starting current until back-EMF builds up
Reverse the motor when its load becomes too high
Hold the motor at a constant speed once it is running
Increase the starting torque by raising the armature current

explanation: At standstill there is no back-EMF, so only the armature's low resistance limits the current. A slow-start resistor keeps that surge down; a centrifugal or time switch then shorts it out so full current is available at speed.

question: An engine rpm indicator using a tacho-generator works because the tacho-generator's output frequency is proportional to engine speed, and the indicator contains:

options.text: A stepper motor, which moves one step per engine revolution
An induction motor, whose speed is set by the supply voltage
A synchronous motor, whose speed follows the supply frequency
A DC series motor, whose speed rises as the load falls

explanation: The small engine-driven alternator produces a frequency proportional to rpm; the synchronous motor in the gauge turns at a speed locked to that frequency and drives the pointer through a magnetic drag cup. Voltage variations do not affect the reading.
